title: The City of Many-Columned Iram
summary: In the reign of the Umayyad Caliph Mu'awiyah, an Arab traveler named Abdullah ibn Qilab was searching for a lost camel in the great south...
full_text:
In the reign of the Umayyad Caliph Mu'awiyah, an Arab traveler named Abdullah ibn Qilab was searching for a lost camel in the great southern wilderness of the Rub al-Khali—the Empty Quarter. As a violent sandstorm cleared, Abdullah beheld a sight that made him doubt his own senses: rising from the red dunes stood the towering walls of a magnificent city, built entirely of golden bricks and silver tiles.

Entering through massive gates of carved sandalwood studded with rubies, Abdullah walked through silent, empty streets lined with colossal palaces supported by thousands of translucent pillars carved from alabaster and chrysolite. In the courtyards flowed clear canals over beds of pearls and emeralds, and trees made of burnished gold bore fruits of amber and turquoise. Yet not a single human footstep broke the silence, and not a single bird sang in the branches.

Filled with awe and dread, Abdullah gathered a handful of pearls from the dry riverbed, mounted his camel, and fled back to the civilized cities of Yemen.

When news of his discovery reached the Caliph, Abdullah was brought to Damascus. The Caliph summoned the venerable sage Ka'ab al-Ahbar and asked: 'Is there truly such a city in the desert, or was this traveler delirious with thirst?'

The sage unrolled ancient chronicles and answered: 'It is the truth, O Commander of the Faithful. That is Iram of the Pillars, built by King Shaddad of the ancient tribe of Ad. In his supreme arrogance, Shaddad sought to build a paradise on earth that would rival the celestial heavens. For five hundred years, he gathered all the gold, gems, and pearls of the world to build his city. But when he approached its gates to inaugurate his glory, a celestial cry of wrath struck him and his host, and they perished in an instant. The city was swallowed by the drifting sands, hidden forever from human eyes, save for a lone traveler who would find it to remind the mighty that all earthly pride is nothing but passing dust.'
moral: Arrogant pride that builds monuments to rival the heavens vanishes like dust before the desert wind.
